title: CYP2D6 and Tamoxifen: Star Alleles, Activity Score and the Switch
summary: Learn how CYP2D6 star alleles combine into an activity score and metabolizer phenotype, why poor and intermediate metabolizers make less endoxifen on tamoxifen, and what the CPIC 2018 guideline recommends instead of simply raising the dose.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 75 Hits 1, 6, 14, 15 and 17 and Trap 5 (CYP2D6/tamoxifen cluster). Checked against the CPIC 2018 CYP2D6-tamoxifen guideline recommendations (Goetz 2018, quoted verbatim in Olivera 2019, read via full text), Schroth 2017 (34–52% endoxifen variability), Gaedigk 2018 and Caudle 2017 (activity score and phenotype terms), Taylor 2020 and Zhou 2017 (endoxifen potency; CYP2D6*10). Qualifier: the reviewer’s “CYP2D6*10 (Asians ~50%)” is an East-Asian allele frequency (~50–58%) that differs across Asian subpopulations and conflates allele frequency with metabolizer prevalence (missing-context flag). The “endoxifen up to 10-fold higher than 4-hydroxytamoxifen” plasma comparison is not taught; potency vs parent tamoxifen is taught instead. Not taught: warfarin/clopidogrel, other drug-gene pairs.

objectives: Explain how CYP2D6 star alleles are assigned function values and summed into a diplotype activity score that maps to a metabolizer phenotype.
Relate CYP2D6 poor/intermediate metabolizer status to reduced endoxifen and tamoxifen outcomes.
Apply the CPIC 2018 recommendation for a CYP2D6 poor or intermediate metabolizer on tamoxifen.

scenes.title: Same dose, same protection?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three premenopausal women with early estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer all start adjuvant tamoxifen 20 mg/day. Their CYP2D6 genotypes differ: patient 1 is *1/*1, patient 2 is *4/*4, patient 3 is *10/*10 (East Asian ancestry). The token asks whether an identical dose gives identical protection.

cues.text: Three premenopausal women with early estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer all start the same adjuvant tamoxifen dose: twenty milligrams a day.
But their CYP2D6 genotypes differ: star-one/star-one, star-four/star-four, and star-ten/star-ten.
Same tablet, same dose. Same protection?

scenes.title: From star allele to phenotype
scenes.altText: Schematic of CYP2D6 genotype interpretation. Star-allele nomenclature: *1 is the reference/normal-function haplotype; higher star numbers are identifiers, not function ranks — a numbered allele may be normal, decreased, no, or increased function. The activity score assigns each allele a value (no function 0, decreased 0.5, normal 1; a gene duplication multiplies by copy number), and the sum of both alleles gives the diplotype activity score, which maps to poor, intermediate, normal, or ultrarapid metabolizer. A tamoxifen schematic shows CYP2D6 converting tamoxifen to endoxifen, the main active metabolite.

cues.text: Start with the names. Star-one is the reference, normal-function allele. Every higher star number is only an identifier: it may mark a normal, decreased, no-function, or even increased-function allele. The number does not rank the function.

So each allele is given a function value: zero for no function, one-half for decreased, one for normal, and a duplicated allele is multiplied by its copy number. Add the two alleles and you get the diplotype activity score.
That score maps to a phenotype: poor, intermediate, normal, or ultrarapid metabolizer.
For tamoxifen this matters, because CYP2D6 converts it to endoxifen, the principal active metabolite.

scenes.title: Low CYP2D6, low endoxifen, higher risk
scenes.altText: Schematic linking genotype to outcome. Endoxifen is the main active antiestrogen, roughly one hundred times more potent than parent tamoxifen. CYP2D6 diplotype explains about 34 to 52 percent of the variability in endoxifen concentrations, so poor and intermediate metabolizers reach lower endoxifen and, in some adjuvant studies, have a higher risk of recurrence. CYP2D6*10 is a decreased-function allele and the most common CYP2D6 allele in East Asian populations (allele frequency roughly one half), so *10/*10 is an intermediate-metabolizer genotype.

cues.text: Endoxifen is the heavy hitter: it is a far more potent antiestrogen than tamoxifen itself, by roughly a hundredfold. So the amount of endoxifen a patient makes is what counts.

CYP2D6 genotype explains about thirty-four to fifty-two percent of the variation in endoxifen levels. Poor and intermediate metabolizers make less endoxifen, and in some adjuvant studies they have a higher risk of recurrence.
Star-ten is a decreased-function allele, and it is the most common CYP2D6 allele in East Asian populations, with an allele frequency near one half.
So a star-ten/star-ten patient is an intermediate metabolizer, not a normal one, even on the standard dose.

scenes.title: What CPIC says to do
scenes.altText: Decision schematic from the CPIC 2018 tamoxifen guideline. Normal metabolizer: standard tamoxifen 20 mg/day, and avoid strong-to-moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors. Poor or intermediate metabolizer: recommend alternative hormonal therapy — an aromatase inhibitor in postmenopausal women, or an aromatase inhibitor plus ovarian function suppression in premenopausal women, because these are superior to tamoxifen regardless of CYP2D6 genotype. Tamoxifen 40 mg/day is only a fallback when aromatase inhibitors are contraindicated; it raises but does not normalize endoxifen and is insufficient in poor metabolizers and in intermediate metabolizers carrying two reduced-function alleles. Hook answers follow.

cues.text: Here is the CPIC rule. A normal metabolizer gets the standard twenty milligrams a day, and you keep strong CYP2D6 inhibitors off the medication list.

A poor or intermediate metabolizer gets a different drug: an aromatase inhibitor if postmenopausal, or an aromatase inhibitor plus ovarian function suppression if premenopausal. These beat tamoxifen regardless of genotype.
Forty milligrams of tamoxifen is only a fallback when aromatase inhibitors are contraindicated. It raises endoxifen but does not normalize it, and it is not enough in poor metabolizers.
Back to the hook: patient one continues standard tamoxifen; patients two and three, intermediate or poor, should switch to alternative hormonal therapy.

props.label: 40 mg only if AI contraindicated — not enough in PM

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards. First: a higher star number means worse enzyme function (no — star numbers are identifiers, not a function scale). Second: a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer on tamoxifen should simply be doubled to 40 mg (no — change the drug; 40 mg is only a fallback if aromatase inhibitors are contraindicated). Third: a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor does not matter if the genotype is normal (no — inhibitors phenocopy a poor metabolizer and lower endoxifen).

cues.text: Trap one: a higher star number means worse function. No. Star numbers are identifiers, not a ranking; the function is set by the allele, not its number.
Trap two: a poor metabolizer on tamoxifen should just be doubled to forty milligrams. No. Change the drug to an aromatase inhibitor; forty milligrams is only a fallback.
Trap three: a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor is harmless if the genotype is normal. No. Inhibitors phenocopy a poor metabolizer and drop endoxifen.

scenes.title: Count the copies, then switch
scenes.altText: Memory aid: picture CYP2D6 as a pair of engines converting tamoxifen fuel into endoxifen power. Count the working engines from the two alleles to read the activity score and phenotype; if the engines are weak (poor or intermediate), do not pour in more fuel — switch to a different engine, an aromatase inhibitor. A card lists where the analogy breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: CYP2D6 is a pair of engines turning tamoxifen fuel into endoxifen power. Count the working engines from the two alleles to get the activity score and phenotype.

If the engines are weak, do not pour in more fuel — switch to a different engine, an aromatase inhibitor. Where it breaks: the activity score is a crude, substrate-dependent estimate; star-ten sits on the intermediate-normal border and experts disagree; and genotype explains only part of endoxifen variability.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens summarizing the rule: the diplotype activity score sets the CYP2D6 phenotype, and a poor or intermediate metabolizer on tamoxifen should switch to alternative hormonal therapy rather than simply receiving more drug.

cues.text: Add the two alleles into an activity score to read the CYP2D6 phenotype, and for a poor or intermediate metabolizer on tamoxifen switch to an aromatase inhibitor with ovarian suppression when premenopausal rather than just raising the dose.

props.label: Two alleles → activity score → CYP2D6 phenotype
PM/IM on tamoxifen → switch to AI (±ovarian suppression), not more drug

explanation.what: Plain language: tamoxifen is a pro-drug for its own active form, endoxifen, and the liver enzyme CYP2D6 makes most of it. Genes come in versions called star alleles; adding up the two versions a patient carries tells you whether they make a lot of enzyme, a little, or none, and that decides the drug plan. Scientific terms: CYP2D6, star (*) allele nomenclature, reference/normal-function allele (*1), activity score (AS), diplotype, poor/intermediate/normal/ultrarapid metabolizer (PM/IM/NM/UM), endoxifen, 4-hydroxytamoxifen, aromatase inhibitor (AI), ovarian function suppression.
explanation.why: Endoxifen is the principal active antiestrogen and far more potent than parent tamoxifen, so patients who cannot form it (PM/IM) are underexposed. Because aromatase inhibitors do not depend on CYP2D6 and outperform tamoxifen regardless of genotype, switching the drug is more reliable than pushing the tamoxifen dose.
explanation.measure: Allele function values: no function 0, decreased 0.5, normal 1; a gene duplication multiplies by copy number. The sum of both alleles is the diplotype activity score, which maps to PM (lowest), IM, NM, or UM (highest). CYP2D6 genotype explains ~34–52% of endoxifen variability. Standard adjuvant tamoxifen is 20 mg/day; 40 mg/day is an FDA-approved higher dose used only as a fallback.
explanation.differs: Star number (an identifier) vs allele function (normal/decreased/no/increased); endoxifen (main active metabolite) vs 4-hydroxytamoxifen (minor); CYP2D6*10 (decreased function, common in East Asians) vs *1 (reference); genotype-based PM vs drug-induced (phenocopied) PM from a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: translate a diplotype into a phenotype, recognize that a higher star number is not a worse allele, pick alternative hormonal therapy (not a doubled dose) for a PM/IM on tamoxifen, or spot a CYP2D6 inhibitor phenocopying a poor metabolizer.

mnemonic.text: CYP2D6 is a pair of engines turning tamoxifen fuel into endoxifen power: count the working engines from the two alleles to read the activity score and phenotype, and if the engines are weak, switch to a different engine (an aromatase inhibitor) rather than pouring in more fuel.
mnemonic.explanation: Links diplotype counting to phenotype and to the switch-the-drug rule.
mnemonic.limitation: The activity score is a crude, substrate-dependent estimate; CYP2D6*10 sits on the IM/NM border and classification is debated; genotype explains only ~34–52% of endoxifen variability, so other factors (inhibitors, adherence, CYP3A) matter.

questions.stem: A premenopausal woman with early estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer is a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer (*4/*4) and is starting adjuvant tamoxifen 20 mg/day. Which management best matches the CPIC 2018 recommendation?

options.text: Switch to an aromatase inhibitor plus ovarian function suppression
options.rationale: Correct. CPIC recommends alternative hormonal therapy for CYP2D6 poor/intermediate metabolizers; in premenopausal women that is an aromatase inhibitor with ovarian function suppression.

options.text: Double the tamoxifen to 40 mg/day as first choice
options.rationale: Incorrect. 40 mg/day is only a fallback if aromatase inhibitors are contraindicated; it raises but does not normalize endoxifen and is insufficient in poor metabolizers.
Incorrect. A poor metabolizer forms little endoxifen, so standard tamoxifen is the weaker option here.
Incorrect. Paroxetine is a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor and would further lower endoxifen.

questions.stem: A patient is genotyped as CYP2D6 *4/*5, where *4 and *5 are both no-function alleles. Using the activity-score system, what is the predicted metabolizer phenotype?

options.rationale: Correct. Two no-function alleles each score 0, giving a diplotype activity score of 0, the poor-metabolizer phenotype.
Incorrect. Ultrarapid status requires increased-function alleles or gene duplication, not two no-function alleles.
Incorrect. A normal metabolizer needs roughly full-function alleles; two no-function alleles cannot give that.
Incorrect. Intermediate status reflects reduced but not absent function; two no-function alleles give no activity.

questions.stem: A CYP2D6 normal metabolizer stable on tamoxifen is started on paroxetine for hot flashes. What is the main pharmacogenetic concern?

options.text: Paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6 and phenocopies a poor metabolizer, lowering endoxifen
options.rationale: Correct. A strong CYP2D6 inhibitor reproduces the poor-metabolizer phenotype and reduces endoxifen formation.

options.text: Paroxetine induces CYP2D6 and raises endoxifen to toxic levels
options.rationale: Incorrect. Paroxetine inhibits, it does not induce, CYP2D6.

options.text: No concern, because the genotype is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Drug-induced inhibition overrides a normal genotype, so the genotype no longer protects endoxifen formation.

options.text: Paroxetine changes the patient’s CYP2D6 star alleles
options.rationale: Incorrect. A drug cannot alter inherited star alleles; it alters enzyme activity, not genotype.

references.usedFor: Full text (Europe PMC). CPIC 2018 tamoxifen recommendations quoted: NM start tamoxifen 20 mg/day and avoid CYP2D6 inhibitors; PM/IM recommend alternative hormonal therapy (aromatase inhibitor postmenopausal; AI + ovarian function suppression premenopausal), superior to tamoxifen regardless of CYP2D6 genotype; 40 mg/day only if AI contraindicated, increases but does not normalize endoxifen; ~90% of tamoxifen demethylated by CYP3A4 then oxidized by CYP2D6 to endoxifen.

claims.text: Star-allele naming: *1 reference/normal; star numbers are identifiers that may denote normal, decreased, no or increased function.
Allele function values (0/0.5/1, duplication multiplies) summed to a diplotype activity score mapping to PM/IM/NM/UM.
Endoxifen is the main active metabolite, ~100-fold more potent than parent tamoxifen; CYP2D6 forms it after CYP3A4 demethylation.
CYP2D6 genotype explains ~34–52% of endoxifen variability; PM/IM form less endoxifen.
CYP2D6*10 is a decreased-function allele and the most common CYP2D6 allele in East Asians (~58% allele frequency).
CPIC 2018: NM standard 20 mg/day; PM/IM alternative hormonal therapy (AI ± ovarian suppression); 40 mg only if AI contraindicated and insufficient in PM; strong CYP2D6 inhibitors phenocopy PM.
Standard adjuvant tamoxifen is 20 mg/day for about 5 years.
Scenario invented; enzyme and metabolite drawings schematic.
“Count the copies, then switch” engine analogy.

accuracyFlags.note: Reviewer Hit 15 gives “CYP2D6*10 (Asians ~50%)”. Published data (Zhou 2017) report *10 as an East-Asian allele frequency near 58% that differs across Asian subpopulations, and the figure is an allele frequency, not the prevalence of the intermediate-metabolizer phenotype; the lesson teaches it as an East-Asian allele frequency.
The management and the 40 mg/day fallback reflect US/international CPIC guidance and FDA-labeled dosing; Philippine regulatory and formulary practice is not covered by these sources.
